claim: Parasites from the genus Plasmodium are responsible for half of a million deaths per year.
source: Parasites from the genus Plasmodium, the causative agents of malaria, are responsible for half of a million deaths per year (WHO, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2018 report

claim: Malaria parasites are becoming resistant to current artemisinin-based therapies.
source: Despite significant effort and money having been devoted for developing vaccines and new preventive treatments, the malaria parasites are becoming resistant to current artemisinin-based therapies (Haldar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haldar et al., 2018

claim: The global death rate from malaria has recently started to rise after many years of decrease.
source: The global death rate from malaria has recently started to rise after many years of decrease (WHO, 2018), emphasizing the necessity to develop new interventions, particularly because climate change may further expand the range of Anopheles mosquitoes (Hertig, 2019; Ryan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2018

claim: Climate change may further expand the range of Anopheles mosquitoes.
source: The global death rate from malaria has recently started to rise after many years of decrease (WHO, 2018), emphasizing the necessity to develop new interventions, particularly because climate change may further expand the range of Anopheles mosquitoes (Hertig, 2019; Ryan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hertig 2019 and Ryan et al. 2020

claim: P. falciparum is the deadliest Plasmodium species that infects humans.
source: The mosquito-borne parasite P. falciparum, the deadliest species that infects humans, alternates between motile and non-motile stages.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Locomotion of apicomplexan parasites occurs by a process called gliding motility.
source: Locomotion of apicomplexan parasites occurs by a process called gliding motility (reviewed in Frénal et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to review by Frénal et al., 2017

claim: The glideosome is anchored in an inner membrane complex located ~25 nm below the parasite plasma membrane.
source: This mode of displacement and the infectivity of the parasite rely on a macromolecular assembly called the glideosome that is anchored in an inner membrane complex located ~25 nm below the parasite plasma membrane (PPM).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: The core of the glideosome consists of an atypical class XIV myosin A (PfMyoA) and a divergent actin (PfAct1).
source: The core of the glideosome consists of an atypical class XIV myosin A (PfMyoA) and a divergent actin (PfAct1).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: PfMyoA binds two light chains: an essential light chain (PfELC) and myosin tail interacting protein (MTIP).
source: PfMyoA is a short myosin with a conserved globular motor domain and a lever arm that binds two light chains: an essential light chain (PfELC) and myosin tail interacting protein (MTIP) (Green et al., 2017; Bookwalter et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Green et al., 2017 and Bookwalter et al., 2017

claim: The N-terminal extension of MTIP binds to integral membrane proteins called GAPs.
source: The N-terminal extension of MTIP binds to integral membrane proteins called GAPs (glideosome associated proteins), which anchors the myosin so that it can interact cyclically with actin (Jones et al., 2012; Figure 1a) (reviewed in Frénal et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones et al., 2012 and review by Frénal et al., 2017

claim: PfMyoA powers fast motility at approximately 2 µm/s during motile sporozoite stages.
source: PfMyoA is a critical molecule in the parasite life-cycle because it powers the fast motility (~2 µm.s−1) required during motile sporozoite stages (Münter et al., 2009), and is essential for providing the force (up to 40 pN) needed for non-motile merozoites to invade erythrocytes (Crick et al., 2014; Robert-Paganin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Münter et al., 2009

claim: PfMyoA provides force up to 40 pN needed for non-motile merozoites to invade erythrocytes.
source: PfMyoA is a critical molecule in the parasite life-cycle because it powers the fast motility (~2 µm.s−1) required during motile sporozoite stages (Münter et al., 2009), and is essential for providing the force (up to 40 pN) needed for non-motile merozoites to invade erythrocytes (Crick et al., 2014; Robert-Paganin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crick et al., 2014 and Robert-Paganin et al., 2019

claim: The crystal structures of full-length PfMyoA in two states of its motor cycle were determined at 2.5 Å and 3.9 Å resolution.
source: We determined the crystal structures of FL PfMyoA with two light chains bound (PfMyoA/PfELC/MTIP-Δn) in the post-rigor (PfMyoA•FL-PR) and in the pre-powerstroke (PfMyoA•FL-PPS) states at 2.5 Å and 3.9 Å resolution, respectively (Supplementary file 1a; Figure 1b and c).
evidence: Experimental data from X-ray crystallography presented in the manuscript

claim: The converter orientation is the same in both the motor domain and the full-length post-rigor structures.
source: The converter orientation is the same in both the motor domain (PfMyoA•MD-PR) (Robert-Paganin et al., 2019) and the FL (PfMyoA•FL-PR) post-rigor structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: Comparison of structural data from current study and previous publication

claim: In the PPS states, the converter orientation is less primed by ~30° in the MD structure compared with the FL structure.
source: In the PPS states, crystallized with ADP and Pi analogs, however, the converter orientation is less primed by ~30° in the MD structure compared with that found in the FL structure (Robert-Paganin et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: Comparison of structural data from current study and previous publication

claim: SAXS experiments validated that the PPS of PfMyoA adopts the more primed orientation in solution.
source: SAXS experiments validated that the PPS of PfMyoA adopts the more primed orientation in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: Experimental SAXS data presented in the manuscript

claim: The priming of the lever arm in the TgMyoA•MD-PPS structure is identical to that of the PfMyoA•FL-PPS structure.
source: Interestingly, the priming of the lever arm in the TgMyoA•MD-PPS structure (Powell et al., 2018) is identical to that of the PfMyoA•FL-PPS structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 4e).
evidence: Comparison of structural data from current study and published structure

claim: The lever arm is more primed in the PPS state of PfMyoA compared with that of conventional myosins, leading to a larger powerstroke than most myosins.
source: Notably, the lever arm is more primed in the PPS state of PfMyoA compared with that of conventional myosins, leading to a larger powerstroke than most myosins.
evidence: Inference from structural comparison data presented in the manuscript

claim: The converter is reoriented ~90° during the PfMyoA powerstroke.
source: The converter is reoriented ~90° during the powerstroke (Figure 1e).
evidence: Calculated from structural data presented in the manuscript

claim: In conventional myosins such as ScMyo2, the converter is reoriented only ~60° during the powerstroke.
source: In conventional myosins, such as ScMyo2, the converter is reoriented only ~60° during the powerstroke (Figure 1f).
evidence: Comparison with published structural data

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal extension enhanced the duty-ratio by greatly slowing ADP release to the extent that it rate-limited the overall ATPase cycle, which is ~14 fold slower than WT.
source: Deletion of the Nter enhanced the duty-ratio (time spent strongly bound to actin) by greatly slowing ADP release to the extent that it rate-limited the overall ATPase cycle, which is ~14 fold slower than WT (Robert-Paganin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The similarity of the ΔNter heavy chain and WT PfMyoA structures (rmsd of 0.415 Å on 993 atoms) indicates that the deletion does not change or alter the protein fold.
source: The similarity of the ΔNter heavy chain and WT PfMyoA structures (rmsd of 0.415 Å on 993 atoms) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b) strongly argues that the dramatic kinetic differences observed between these two constructs are due to an altered equilibrium between the states of the motor cycle (Robert-Paganin et al., 2019).
evidence: Structural comparison data from the manuscript

claim: Serine 19 phosphorylation (SEP19) accelerates ADP release by stabilizing the converter in its rigor orientation through a polar interaction with converterK764.
source: We previously showed that Serine 19 phosphorylation (SEP19) accelerates ADP release by stabilizing the converter in its rigor orientation through a polar interaction with converterK764 but other residues likely modulate these motor properties.
evidence: Reference to previous findings from the authors

claim: The E6R mutation reduces maximal actin-activated ATPase by approximately 2-fold.
source: The effects of the E6R mutation are similar to that observed with mutants disrupting the polar bond between SEP19 and the converter (S19A and K764E) (Robert-Paganin et al., 2019):~2 fold reduced maximal actin-activated ATPase,~2 fold reduced rate of ADP release that is correlated with a reduced speed of moving actin,~3 fold increased ensemble force, and ~2.5 fold faster dissociation of acto-PfMyoA by MgATP (Figure 2b–f, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental kinetic and motility data presented in the manuscript

claim: The E6R mutation reduces the rate of ADP release by approximately 2-fold.
source: The effects of the E6R mutation are similar to that observed with mutants disrupting the polar bond between SEP19 and the converter (S19A and K764E) (Robert-Paganin et al., 2019):~2 fold reduced maximal actin-activated ATPase,~2 fold reduced rate of ADP release that is correlated with a reduced speed of moving actin,~3 fold increased ensemble force, and ~2.5 fold faster dissociation of acto-PfMyoA by MgATP (Figure 2b–f, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental kinetic data presented in the manuscript

claim: The E6R mutation increases ensemble force by approximately 3-fold.
source: The effects of the E6R mutation are similar to that observed with mutants disrupting the polar bond between SEP19 and the converter (S19A and K764E) (Robert-Paganin et al., 2019):~2 fold reduced maximal actin-activated ATPase,~2 fold reduced rate of ADP release that is correlated with a reduced speed of moving actin,~3 fold increased ensemble force, and ~2.5 fold faster dissociation of acto-PfMyoA by MgATP (Figure 2b–f, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental force measurement data presented in the manuscript

claim: The E6R mutation increases dissociation of acto-PfMyoA by MgATP by approximately 2.5-fold.
source: The effects of the E6R mutation are similar to that observed with mutants disrupting the polar bond between SEP19 and the converter (S19A and K764E) (Robert-Paganin et al., 2019):~2 fold reduced maximal actin-activated ATPase,~2 fold reduced rate of ADP release that is correlated with a reduced speed of moving actin,~3 fold increased ensemble force, and ~2.5 fold faster dissociation of acto-PfMyoA by MgATP (Figure 2b–f, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental kinetic data presented in the manuscript

claim: S691G is the only mutant to date that showed faster in vitro motility and faster ADP release than WT.
source: S691G is the only mutant to date that showed faster in vitro motility and faster ADP release than WT, implying that the mutation destabilizes the strong-ADP state (Figure 2b–d, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental motility and kinetic data presented in the manuscript

claim: The maximal actin-activated ATPase activity of S691G was half that of WT and not rate-limited by ADP release.
source: The maximal actin-activated ATPase activity was half that of WT and not rate-limited by ADP release (Figure 2e, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental ATPase data presented in the manuscript

claim: S691 is involved in the communication between the Relay and the SH1 helices by maintaining an electrostatic bond with RelayQ494.
source: S691 is involved in the communication between the Relay and the SH1 helices by maintaining an electrostatic bond with RelayQ494, which is part of the sequence compensation specific to PfMyoA.
evidence: Inference from structural data presented in the manuscript

claim: The S691G mutant has nine-fold higher basal ATPase activity in the absence of actin compared to WT.
source: The nine-fold higher basal ATPase activity in the absence of actin (Supplementary file 1b) indicates that the pre-powerstroke (PPS) state of the mutant is less stable than WT, while the similar rate of dissociation of acto-PfMyoA by MgATP implies that the stability of the rigor state and the transition to PR are like WT (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental ATPase data presented in the manuscript

claim: The S691G mutant retains the ability to undergo conformational transitions when bound to actin under strain, with a modestly enhanced ensemble force (1.4-fold) compared with WT.
source: The mutant retains the ability to undergo conformational transitions when bound to actin under strain, with a modestly enhanced ensemble force (1.4-fold) compared with WT (Figure 2f, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental force measurement data presented in the manuscript

claim: The T586F mutation had relatively little effect on in vitro motility speed or on ADP-release rates compared with WT.
source: This mutation had relatively little effect on in vitro motility speed or on ADP-release rates compared with WT (Figure 2b–d, Supplementary file 1b), despite the fact that the bulkier Phe would likely reduce the mobility around the wedge due to steric hindrance and thus impede the communication between the active site and the lever arm during the lever arm swing.
evidence: Experimental motility and kinetic data presented in the manuscript

claim: The T586F mutant shows approximately 40% faster transition to the PR state compared to WT.
source: The ~40% faster transition to the PR state suggests that rigor is slightly destabilized, while the elevated basal ATPase indicates a reduced stability of the PPS state (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental kinetic data presented in the manuscript

claim: The T586F mutant has reduced maximal actin-activated ATPase activity compared to WT.
source: The reduced maximal actin-activated ATPase activity of the mutant indicates that other transitions in the motor cycle have slowed (Figure 2e, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental ATPase data presented in the manuscript

claim: The T586F mutant's ability to generate motion under force was better than WT.
source: Similar to the other two point mutants (E6R and S691G), its ability to generate motion under force was better than WT, implying more time spent in actin-bound states of the powerstroke (Figure 2f, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental force measurement data presented in the manuscript

claim: PfMyoA is short and lacks a tail domain like other class XIV myosins.
source: PfMyoA, like other class XIV myosins, is short and lacks a tail domain (Foth et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Foth et al., 2006

claim: The C-terminal region of PfMyoA consists of two degenerate IQ motifs (PfIQ1 and PfIQ2) that deviate from the consensus IQ sequence.
source: The C-terminal region of PfMyoA consists of two degenerate IQ motifs (PfIQ1 and PfIQ2) that deviate from the consensus IQ sequence (IQxxxRGxxxR) but are recognized by the native light chains, PfELC and MTIP.
evidence: Structural data and sequence analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: The recognition of PfIQ2 by MTIP has already been described.
source: The recognition of PfIQ2 by MTIP has already been described (Bosch et al., 2006; Bosch et al., 2007; Douse et al., 2012) and involves several residues from the consensus IQ motif sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–e).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: PfELC interacts with the long HC α-helix with its N-lobe in a closed conformation and its C-lobe in a semi-open conformation.
source: PfELC interacts with the long HC α-helix with its N-lobe in a closed conformation and its C-lobe in a semi-open conformation, as it is the case for other ELCs (Figure 3; Houdusse and Cohen, 1995).
evidence: Structural data from the manuscript and comparison with published structures

claim: The C-lobe of PfELC contains an extremely short α5 helix, which consists of only one turn (α5*) followed by a short linker in which a small inserted helix turn forms (α5'*).
source: While the structure of the N-lobe is mostly conserved compared to other ELCs (Figure 3a and b; Houdusse and Cohen, 1996), the C-lobe contains an extremely short α5 helix, which consists of only one turn (α5*) followed by a short linker in which a small inserted helix turn forms (α5'*) (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: Structural data from the manuscript

claim: The inter-lobe linker of PfELC is shorter than canonical ELCs and forms an internal hairpin-like structure that interacts strongly with the N-lobe and does not contact residues of the HC helix.
source: In addition, the inter-lobe linker is shorter than canonical ELCs and forms an internal hairpin-like structure, that interacts strongly with the N-lobe and does not contact residues of the HC helix (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: Structural data from the manuscript

claim: The unusual inter-lobe linker structure prevents the PfELC from fully surrounding the HC helix.
source: This unusual feature for an inter-lobe linker prevents the PfELC from fully surrounding the HC helix.
evidence: Inference from structural data presented in the manuscript

claim: PfIQ1 is highly degenerate, containing none of the consensus IQ motif residues (IQxxxRGxxxR).
source: PfIQ1 is highly degenerate, containing none of the consensus IQ motif residues (IQxxxRGxxxR) (Figure 4a; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, b and c).
evidence: Sequence analysis and structural data presented in the manuscript

claim: In PfMyoA, the glutamine and proximal arginine of the consensus IQ motif are replaced by a valine (V781) and a glutamate (E785), respectively.
source: In particular, PfIQ1 lacks the glutamine and the proximal arginine that makes specific polar interactions with the C-lobe intra-lobe linker (between α6 and α7) in other myosins (Houdusse and Cohen, 1996; Figure 4b). In PfMyoA, these two residues are replaced by a valine (V781) and a glutamate (E785), respectively (Figure 4c).
evidence: Structural comparison data from the manuscript

claim: The IQ1 motif starts one residue earlier in the PfMyoA HC sequence compared to other myosins because a HC residue is missing in the pliant region at the end of the converter.
source: Interestingly, compared to other myosins, the IQ1 motif starts one residue earlier in the PfMyoA HC sequence because a HC residue is missing in the pliant region at the end of the converter.
evidence: Structural comparison and sequence analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: An atypical Trp (W777) in the PfIQ1 helix strengthens the hydrophobic interactions between PfIQ1 and PfELC.
source: An atypical Trp (W777) in this helix strengthens the hydrophobic interactions between PfIQ1 and PfELC (Figure 4d and e).
evidence: Structural data from the manuscript

claim: In PfMyoA, W777 is sandwiched between the α5*, α5'* and α6 helices, thus interacting with the hydrophobic core of the PfELC C-lobe.
source: In PfMyoA, W777 is sandwiched between the α5*, α5'* and α6 helices, thus interacting with the hydrophobic core of the PfELC C-lobe (Figure 4e).
evidence: Structural data from the manuscript

claim: The absence of electron density for the two helical turns of α5* and α5'* in the PR crystal structure indicates that lack of stabilization by the converter and the W777 side chain affects the fold of these atypical PfELC structural elements.
source: The absence of electron density for the two helical turns of α5* and α5'* in this crystal structure indicates that lack of stabilization by the converter and the W777 side chain affects the fold of these atypical PfELC structural elements (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d, Figure 5a).
evidence: Structural data from the manuscript

claim: TgELC1 and TgELC2 are homologous to classical ELCs and do not display the specific inter-lobe linker nor the atypical α5* and α5'* helices found in PfELC.
source: Interestingly, TgELC1 and TgELC2 are homologous to classical ELCs and do not display the specific inter-lobe linker nor the atypical α5* and α5'* helices found in PfELC, which are also part of the interface with the Converter.
evidence: Comparison with published structures

claim: PfELC does not bind to the HC in the absence of MTIP.
source: The structure of PfELC and its specific association with the HC and MTIP also explains the cooperative binding of these elements and why PfELC does not bind to the HC in the absence of MTIP (Bookwalter et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bookwalter et al., 2017 and inference from structural data

claim: The converter/N-term subdomain interface is key for stabilization of the atypical priming of PfMyoA in the PPS state.
source: To test the hypothesis that this Converter/N-term interface is key for stabilization of the atypical priming of PfMyoA in the PPS state, we designed the triple mutant R707A/E711A/Y714A in silico. As expected, molecular dynamics show that the three mutations destabilize the Converter/Nterm subdomain interface and cause a loss of priming, demonstrating that this interface stabilizes the atypical priming of PfMyoA in the PPS state (Figure 6c, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: Both triple mutants (R707A/E711A/Y714A and R707L/E711R/Y714A) greatly reduce the maximum actin-activated ATPase to ~30% of WT.
source: Both triple mutants greatly impact and tune the properties of the motor similarly: they reduce the maximum actin-activated ATPase to ~30% of WT, and decrease both in vitro motility speed and the ADP release rate to a similar extent (~35% of WT) (Figure 2b–e, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–d, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental ATPase data presented in the manuscript

claim: Both triple mutants (R707A/E711A/Y714A and R707L/E711R/Y714A) decrease both in vitro motility speed and the ADP release rate to ~35% of WT.
source: Both triple mutants greatly impact and tune the properties of the motor similarly: they reduce the maximum actin-activated ATPase to ~30% of WT, and decrease both in vitro motility speed and the ADP release rate to a similar extent (~35% of WT) (Figure 2b–e, Figure 6—figure supplement 1a–d, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Experimental motility and kinetic data presented in the manuscript

claim: Treatment with rapamycin, inducing DiCre dimerization and gene excision, led to PfELC gene truncation.
source: Treatment with rapamycin, inducing DiCre dimerization and gene excision, led to gene truncation (as validated by PCR Figure 7—figure supplement 1b). Truncation was also confirmed by immunoblot and immunofluorescence assay (Figure 7b, c and d).
evidence: Experimental data from PCR, immunoblot, and immunofluorescence assays

claim: Analysis of rapamycin-treated parasites was associated with a near complete ablation of red blood cell invasion over 60 hr of an asexual growth cycle.
source: Analysis of rapamycin-treated parasites was associated with a near complete ablation of red blood cell invasion over 60 hr of an asexual growth cycle, on a par with inhibition levels seen with the non-specific invasion inhibitor heparin (Boyle et al., 2010; Figure 7e).
evidence: Experimental invasion assay data presented in the manuscript

claim: Analysis over a single 48 hr or double 96 hr cycle showed that inhibition of invasion following PfELC truncation was near total.
source: Further analysis over a single 48 hr or double 96 hr cycle showed that this inhibition of invasion was near total (Figure 7f and g) suggesting residual invasion after a single cycle is likely the result of incomplete gene excision.
evidence: Experimental invasion assay data presented in the manuscript

claim: PfELC is essential for asexual blood-stage life-cycle progression.
source: The level of invasion retardation following loss of PfELC suggests that, like the heavy chain PfMyoA (Robert-Paganin et al., 2019), PfELC is essential for asexual blood-stage life-cycle progression.
evidence: Inference from experimental invasion assay data and comparison with previous study

claim: Unlike T. gondii, there is no evidence for redundancy in essential light chains in P. falciparum.
source: Unlike T. gondii, there is no evidence for redundancy in essential light chains.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing complete loss of invasion upon PfELC truncation

claim: The lever arm of PfMyoA is ~30° more primed upon reattachment to the actin track than it is in conventional class II myosins.
source: Unexpectedly, the lever arm of PfMyoA is ~30° more primed upon reattachment to the actin track than it is in conventional class II myosins.
evidence: Structural comparison data presented in the manuscript

claim: Myo10 and Myo1c are two motors for which the lever arm priming position is also large in the PPS.
source: Myo10 and Myo1c are two motors for which the lever arm priming position is also large in the PPS (Ropars et al., 2016), (Münnich et al., 2014), but their lever arm orientation is stabilized by a different set of interactions when compared with PfMyoA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Comparison with published structures

claim: TgELC is a poor model for PfELC considering the low sequence identity (20% and 21% between PfELC and TgELC and TgELC2, respectively).
source: Atomic structures of the PfMyoA lever arm indicate how degenerate IQ motifs of the HC are recognized by PfELC and MTIP, as well as how unusual apolar interactions occur between PfELC and the converter. These unusual features could not have been predicted from recently solved TgMyoA structures of the lever arm bound to TgELC or TgELC2 (Pazicky et al., 2019), because TgELC is a poor model for PfELC considering the low sequence identity (20% and 21% between PfELC and TgELC and TgELC2, respectively).
evidence: Sequence comparison data

claim: PfMyoA lacking the ELC moves actin at half the speed of the motor containing both light chains.
source: PfMyoA lacking the ELC moves actin at half the speed of the motor containing both light chains (Bookwalter et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bookwalter et al., 2017

claim: Video microscopy showed that PfELC cKO merozoites can still deform red blood cells, unlike cKO of PfMyoA heavy chain.
source: It should be noted that video microscopy showed that PfELC cKO merozoites can still deform red blood cells, unlike cKO of PfMyoA heavy chain (Blake et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Blake et al., 2020

claim: cKO of either PfMyoA or PfELC left merozoites entirely incapable of invasion.
source: Nonetheless, cKO of either PfMyoA or PfELC left merozoites entirely incapable of invasion.
evidence: Experimental invasion assay data presented in the manuscript and cited study

claim: Both PfMyoA motor domain and PfELC represent attractive targets for arresting parasite invasion in pathogenic blood stages.
source: Both PfMyoA motor domain and PfELC thus represent attractive targets for arresting parasite invasion in pathogenic blood stages.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing essentiality of both components

claim: The structures provide a precise blueprint for designing small molecules that could prevent binding of PfELC or target PfMyoA full-length motor activity.
source: Importantly, the structures described here provide a precise blueprint for designing just such small molecules that could prevent binding of PfELC or target PfMyoA full-length motor activity and thus diminish glideosome function.
evidence: Inference from structural data presented in the manuscript

claim: The priming of PfMyoA lever arm is maintained throughout the molecular dynamics simulation time course.
source: The first insight from this experiment is that priming of the PfMyoA lever arm is maintained throughout the time course. Even if the lever arm position slightly diverges at the beginning of the simulation, the priming is restored quickly and thus stays stable during the entire simulation (Video 1).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: The converter/PfELC and PfELC/MTIP interfaces are rigid during molecular dynamics simulation.
source: As expected, the converter/PfELC and PfELC/MTIP interfaces are rigid. All the hydrophobic interactions between PfELC and MTIP are maintained during the simulation and the Converter/PfELC interface is more rigid as compared with conventional myosins (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: The PfMyoA lever arm is more rigid than in conventional myosins.
source: We conclude that the priming seen in the PfMyoA•FL-PPS crystal structure is stable, and that the PfMyoA lever arm is more rigid than in conventional myosins.
evidence: Inference from molecular dynamics simulation data

claim: The atypical priming of the PfMyoA lever arm in the PPS state results from several interactions between the lever arm and the motor domain that are not present in conventional myosins.
source: The atypical priming of the PfMyoA lever arm in the PPS state results from several interactions between the lever arm and the motor domain that are not present in conventional myosins.
evidence: Structural comparison data presented in the manuscript

claim: Conformational changes at the end of the SH1 helix are required to allow an additional Converter rotation so that it can reach the PfMyoA motor domain surface with which it interacts.
source: Conformational changes at the end of the SH1 helix are required to allow an additional Converter rotation so that it can reach the PfMyoA motor domain surface with which it interacts (Figure 1—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: Inference from structural data presented in the manuscript

claim: The interface between the Converter and the N-terminal subdomain is highly stable and maintained throughout the molecular dynamics time course.
source: Interestingly, interactions between PfELC, loop-1 and the β-bulge are highly labile during molecular dynamics (Video 1), but the interface between the Converter and the N-term subdomain is highly stable and maintained throughout the time course (Video 1).
evidence: Molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript

claim: A kink of approximately 130° occurs in the HC helix between the two IQ motifs of the PfMyoA lever arm.
source: Interestingly, this interaction is possible only after the formation of a ~ 130° kink in the HC helix between the two IQs motifs of the PfMyoA lever arm.
evidence: Structural data from the manuscript

claim: The kink in the HC helix between the two IQ motifs is facilitated by proline (HCP802).
source: The kink is facilitated by proline (HCP802) and is similar in all molecules of the asymmetric units of the structural states we crystallized (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: Structural data from the manuscript

claim: The contacts at the MTIP/PfELC interface contribute to stabilizing the kink and providing a specific conserved feature for this rather rigid lever arm.
source: The contacts at the MTIP/PfELC interface contribute to stabilizing the kink and providing a specific conserved feature for this rather rigid lever arm.
evidence: Inference from structural data presented in the manuscript

claim: Integration of the introns into the PfELC gene did not affect parasite asexual growth.
source: Integration of the introns did not affect parasite asexual growth (Figure 7a).
evidence: Experimental growth curve data presented in the manuscript

claim: The 'folded-back' position of the lever arm in the PR state is not primarily populated in solution and is selected by crystal contacts.
source: SAXS experiments demonstrate that this 'folded-back' position of the lever arm is not primarily populated in solution and is selected by crystal contacts. In solution, the lever arm adopts an extended conformation as seen in other myosins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d and e–h).
evidence: SAXS experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Myo10 undergoes a large ~140° swing during the powerstroke.
source: In comparison, Myo10 undergoes a large ~140° swing during the powerstroke (Ropars et al., 2016) linked to both a highly primed lever arm orientation in its PPS state and an unusual rigor converter position.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ropars et al., 2016

claim: The absence of the ELC in skeletal muscle myosin results in a twofold reduction in isometric force.
source: This is in contrast to what was seen with skeletal muscle myosin, in which the absence of the ELC results in a twofold reduction in isometric force (VanBuren et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to VanBuren et al., 1994
